files.text:
In 1787 Ernst Florens Friedrich Chladni, a lawyer’s son from Wittenberg who had taken a degree in law to please his father and then given it up for physics, published a short book in Leipzig called Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges, discoveries in the theory of sound. He had been working at a trick for years. He held a thin square plate of glass or brass still at one point, scattered sand over it, and drew a violin bow down its edge. The plate sang, and the sand moved. It jumped away from the parts of the plate that were swinging and came to rest along the lines that stood still, so that in a second or two the note had drawn its own picture. Touch the edge with a fingertip somewhere else, bow at another place, and a higher note drew a different figure.

He had no camera and no way to fix the sand, so he copied each figure by eye, and a Leipzig engraver, Capieux, cut them in copper: well over a hundred of them on eleven plates at the back of the book, numbered, with small letters for the places where he had held the plate and where the bow went. This is the eighth sheet, twenty square plates, figures 87 to 106, from the Getty Research Institute’s copy.

Look at the drawings closely and they are full of sand. The cross of figure 87 swells at its centre into a dark star, because grains run along a nodal line and pile up where two lines meet; the eight rays of figure 99 meet in a heap. The lines are thin where the plate crosses them steeply and wide where it barely moves on either side. Chladni did not invent any of this. He drew what the sand did.

He spent the rest of his life on the road with his plates and the glass instruments he built, earning his keep from lectures in Europe’s drawing rooms. In 1808 he brought them to Paris. Early the next year Laplace and the physicists of the Institut presented him to Napoleon, who watched the sand gather, asked questions, gave Chladni six thousand francs to publish his Traité d’acoustique in French, and had the Institut set a prize, a medal of a kilogram of gold, for a mathematical theory of vibrating elastic surfaces that would agree with experiment.

Most of the mathematicians in Paris thought it could not be done, and only one person entered. Sophie Germain had taught herself mathematics from her father’s library and had sent her work to Lagrange under a man’s name. Her first memoir, in 1811, was turned down: its calculus had mistakes, though Lagrange, one of the judges, worked the right equation out of her assumptions. Her second, in 1813, got an honourable mention. Her third won the prize in January 1816, the first the Academy had given to a woman. She did not go to the ceremony. Her conditions for a free edge were still not right; Kirchhoff settled them in 1850, and in 1909 Walther Ritz at last computed the figures of a free square plate well enough to set beside Chladni’s sand.

# chladni-slider Ernst Chladni's own sand figures, made again as you scroll. The sheet is Tab. VIII of his *Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges* (Leipzig 1787): twenty square plates, figures 87 to 106, engraved in copper by Capieux in 1786. It begins as bare, toned rag paper inside its ruled border. Then all twenty plates come alive together, the whole sheet always in view, with only a faint ripple across it from the top left: each plate's square is ruled, sand is sifted over it from a moving hand, and the bow is drawn: the grains hop out of the parts of the plate that swing and gather, in a second or two, on the lines that stand still, which here are the engraving's own lines. Where three or four lines cross they creep together into the heaps Chladni drew as dark stars. Then the printed line comes up out of the sand, from the heaviest heap outward, each grain going as the ink reaches it, and the number and letters are cut last. After the twentieth figure the title and the engraver's line follow, and the last frame is the scan, pixel for pixel. Scroll back and it un-makes. The folder keeps its old name; it is no longer a slider. One input: scroll. ```html
``` ```js import { chladniSlider } from './chladni-slider.js'; const destroy = chladniSlider(section, { runway: 300 }); destroy.seek(0.42); // show a moment at once (tests, figure sheets) destroy.progress; // where the sheet is now, 0..1 destroy.running; // true only while the spring is catching up with the scroll destroy(); // removes the canvas, listeners, observers, GL objects ``` Without JS, without WebGL2, or with reduced motion, the section is the ``: the finished sheet lying on the page with a tight shadow. ## Options | data- / option | default | what it does | | --- | --- | --- | | `src` | (required) | the sheet's JSON; `.webp`, `-paper.webp`, `-times.webp`, `-sand.webp` sit beside it | | `runway` | `300` | the section's height in svh while live (the time the scroll has to make the sheet) | | `grains` | `1` | multiplier on the sand density (grains are counted from the plate's size on screen, then scaled by its line length, x0.7 to x1.35) | Events (bubbling, forward scrolling only), for sound later: `chladni:bow` `{fig}` as the bow starts on a plate, `chladni:figure` `{fig}` when its line has printed, `chladni:done`. ## The real thing Chladni held a thin square plate of glass or brass at one point (a fingertip or a clamp), dusted it evenly with sand, damped one or two places on the edge with his fingers and drew a rosined bow down the edge somewhere else. The note sounds at once and the sand starts to jump. A grain is thrown only where the plate's acceleration beats gravity, so it leaves the antinodes in small hops that shorten as it nears a line that stands still, and within a second or two the sand lies in lines: thin where the plate's slope across them is steep, wide where it barely moves on either side, and heaped where lines cross. He had no way to fix it, so he drew each figure by eye; Capieux engraved them, ruling the square first and cutting the number and the letters (keyed to his text, for where the plate was held and bowed) last. What the piece models: the order (square, sand, bow, the line, the letters), the sand's physics (below), the heaps at crossings, the sheet's own paper and ink. What it simplifies: the plate is never shown as glass or brass; the sand lies on the engraving's paper, so that the figure it settles into can become the print in place. The bow itself is the scroll. ## How it works **Offline (Python, in the scratch folder: `s1_layers.py`, `s2_maps.py`, about 300 lines).** 1. *Optical density.* The scan in linear light against a local paper estimate (median of a 1/8 downscale); ink is anything denser than paper by 0.16 that contains a core denser than 0.55, and is not a speck. 2. *The paper before printing.* Every ink pixel and an 11 px halo is refilled with real paper texture copied from a clean offset nearby (29 to 131 px away, in rounds for the wide heaps), colour-matched by a normalised Gaussian estimate of the local paper and feathered into the scan. A maximum of fill and scan is taken only in the ink's core: taking it everywhere brightened a ring round every line, a ghost of the figure that the absence test caught. The rings now sit within half a grey level of the paper around them. 3. *The plates.* Long strokes found by morphological opening locate the twenty squares to a pixel. Inside each, ink components are nodal lines, letters (small, free-standing) or paper scratches (faint); outside, numbers and letters go to the nearest plate, the double border and the title and engraver's line to their own classes. Unclassed ink (specks, the dark edge of the leaf) is paper and is there from the start. 4. *Arrival times.* Each square is ruled clockwise from its top-left corner. Each figure's lines print by geodesic distance along the ink (`MCP_Geometric`) from their thickest point, the heap, with a little fBm in the front. Letters left to right. Packed at half resolution, lossless: R = time inside its stage, G = class. 5. *Sand fields.* On a 128 grid over each plate: `d`, the distance to Chladni's lines, and `dr`, the distance to the ridges between them (the medial axis of the free plate, and the free edge, which swings most). `A = sin(pi/2 * d / (d + dr))`, 0 on his lines and 1 on the ridges: a stand-in for the mode's amplitude drawn from his own figure rather than fitted. The G channel holds, for every cell, the time the nearest line ink prints, so a grain knows when to go. Heaps are where the line ink is much thicker than a ruled line (figs 87, 88, 99, 101, plus small ones at some crossings). **Runtime (WebGL2, one canvas).** - *The sheet* is one fragment shader: per pixel, `colour = P * (O / P)^a` in linear light, where `P` is the paper before printing, `O` the scan and `a` how much of the ink has arrived, from the pixel's class, its time and that stage's progress. When every `a` is 1 the result is the scan. Nothing is cross-faded; a line that has not arrived is absent. - *The sand* is the random walk from the old version of this component, now driven by each plate's field: under a threshold (about one g) a grain stays put; above it, it hops a distance that grows with the amplitude, with a small drift down the amplitude slope (a grain landing on a plate tilted as it swings is kicked downhill a little more often). Grains already on a line still tremble and creep toward a heap, where they roll over each other into a mound. Nothing places a grain on a line. The walk runs once per plate from a fixed seed (240 steps, kept as 25 snapshots, computed in an idle callback just before it is needed), so scroll can play it both ways; between snapshots, a grain still ringing is lifted and nudged by a hash of the moment, so it dances while you scroll and is still when you stop. - *Each grain* is a point sprite: washed river sand (warm quartz, iron-stained, the odd dark mineral), lit as a small translucent dome from a low window at the upper left, with a shadow that lengthens as it leaves the paper. A grain shrinks to nothing as the ink reaches the place it lies; a grain left out in the field is brushed off early in the printing. - *No camera, at any size.* The whole sheet always fits the viewport (contain, with a margin), pinned while the runway scrolls. All twenty plates run the same schedule at once, offset by a ripple of under 3.5% of the runway. Grains are sized to the sheet as shown (never under 1.7 device px) and counted so a freshly sifted plate is about a fifth covered. - *Scroll is time*: a pinned stage on a 300svh runway, a critically damped spring toward the scroll position, and the loop stops when it has caught up. Nothing runs at rest, off screen, or in a hidden tab. ## Theming The page colour around the sheet is the section's computed `background-color` (`--paper`, `#f3f0e8`). `--cl-gutter` sets the stage's side padding (6px on a phone in the demo). The sheet itself is never recoloured. ## Accessibility The art is ornament: the `` has `alt=""` and `aria-hidden`, the canvas `aria-hidden`. The essay around it carries the content. Vertical swipes scroll the page; nothing captures touch. ## Reduced motion The printed sheet, still: the ``, with no runway and no canvas. ## Cost Assets 2.5 MB (scan 1.26 MB, paper 0.86 MB, times 0.21 MB, sand fields 0.22 MB). The scan and paper are uploaded at the size they are shown (mipmapped), the times map once, exactly. A plate's walk takes 20-60 ms once; all twenty plates have sand at once (about 80,000 sprites on a large screen, 25,000 on a phone; under 2 ms a frame on an M1). Idle: zero. ## Credits The sheet: Chladni, *Entdeckungen über die Theorie des Klanges*, Leipzig 1787, Tab. VIII, engraved by Capieux; Getty Research Institute copy, scanned by the Internet Archive (`entdeckungenuber00chla`), public domain. Details in `assets/credits.json`.
